title: Curriculum started
text: Every earlier attempt at proper walking had to find balance, alternating steps and forward progress at once, and settled for a shortcut each time: skipping with one leg as a prop (v3, v4, v5-warm), stumbling forward with alternating steps and falling (v5-fresh), or standing still (v6). The curriculum gives each skill its own training reward: 1 balance, 2 step (alternating feet, even in place), 3 walk, 4 walk fast. Each stage starts from the previous stage's champion. Attempt 1 started Wednesday 08:15. Running alongside for comparison: v7-alt, which starts from the alternating stumbler and has to learn balance while walking.

title: v7-alt stopped; the curriculum gets the whole machine
text: v7-alt (warm start from the alternating stumbler, with the per-distance gait tax) kept alternating, with foot 2 leading about 52% of the time and roughly 15 front-foot changes per episode, but after 177 generations every training episode still ended in a fall around x = 14. It is kept below as a comparison but no longer trains, so the curriculum runs alone on the four cores. The local dashboard on port 8771 now follows whichever curriculum stage is active.

title: Attempt 1 found a shortcut: tapping in a split stance. Attempt 2 started.
text: Stage 1 of attempt 1 passed, but its champion balances with its feet 2.9 units apart, foot 2 always in front: the skipper's stance. Stage 2 then learned to tap its feet alternately in that stance: about 70 alternating touchdowns per episode and zero front-foot changes, so the feet never pass each other, and the search has stopped exploring (σ 0.013). Attempt 2 fixes both: stage 1 now also pays for keeping the feet together, and stage 2 only counts a touchdown as a step when the foot coming down is the front foot and the legs alternate. Under the new step reward the tapper drops from 105 to 47 points while a real stepper can earn about 300. Attempt 1 keeps running as the baseline.

title: Attempt 1 stopped; attempt 3 starts stepping from the stumbler
text: Attempt 1's stepping stage never stopped tapping: for over 200 generations it made zero front-foot changes, with its feet split almost one unit apart, and its search had stopped exploring, so I stopped it at generation 454. I also found that the plateau watcher had quit at 08:29 because it didn't know about the curriculum scripts; it's fixed and running again. Attempt 2 is still in its balance stage: no falls, body level, but the feet are 0.53 units apart and the pass test wants under 0.4. With the freed cores, attempt 3 skips balance and starts the real-steps stage from v5-fresh, the one walker that already swaps its feet about 17 times per episode. It only has to learn not to fall while stepping.

title: Attempts 2 and 3 stuck on opposite sides; attempt 4 adds training wheels
text: Attempt 2's stepping stage chose to stand still with its feet together: about one front-foot change per episode, because a step that falls costs more than standing earns. Attempt 3 did the opposite: it kept the alternating stumble, with about seventeen front-foot changes, but fell on all twenty test tracks at x ≈ 17, through both the step and the walk stage. Both were stopped. Attempt 4 uses training wheels: an upright torque on the body that keeps it from tipping, faded out over four stages (support 2, 1, 0.5, then none), followed by walking fast in the real game. With support 2 the stumbler never falls. Eighteen generations in, the best candidate already makes about eighty real crossing steps in an episode, foot 2 leads about 59% of the time, and it walks forward. The real test is whether the gait survives as the support is removed.

title: GOAL MET: training wheels taught it to walk with alternating feet
text: Attempt 4 worked. The support stages passed one after another, each in about an hour: support 2 after 68 generations, support 1 after 62, support 0.5 after 58. Then the real test, no support at all, passed at 14:15: on twenty held-out tracks, no falls, it reached the finish every time, 128 front-foot changes per run, and foot 2 led only a little over half the time. The goal check, on twenty different tracks, passes on every requirement for both the walk champion (257.5) and the walk-fast champion (264.1). On a hundred unseen tracks the walk-fast champion scores 263.9 with a spread of only ±1.1, no falls, and finishes all hundred in about 22 seconds each. Compared with the old skipping walker on the same hundred tracks: about 124 front-foot changes per run against almost none, 2 falls against 7, but about 10 points lower (260 vs 270), because alternating steps cost more motor effort. The walk-fast stage keeps training to make it faster and cheaper.

title: Still improving: attempt 5 polishes the walker
text: The walk-fast stage of attempt 4 keeps improving, but slowly: its held-out champion went from 267 to 276 over about an hour, with no falls and the feet sharing the lead about fifty-fifty, while its search is narrowing (σ 0.015). The plateau rule will probably end it soon. Its main weakness is effort: about 99 points of motor effort per run, against 75 for the old skipper, which is why the skipper still scores about ten points more. Attempt 5 starts from this champion and makes effort count one and a half times in training, with the real fall cost and the same gait tax, a smaller step size and a larger population for fine-tuning. Both run side by side.

title: Check-in: both runs progressing, nothing changed
text: Attempt 4's walk-fast champion holds at 275.8 on the held-out tracks with no falls and the feet sharing the lead (foot 2 in front 54% of the time); it gained 7.4 points over the last 200 generations, just above the plateau threshold of 5, and its step size keeps shrinking (σ 0.012). Attempt 5 (effort counts 1.5 times) started eight minutes ago and is still at generation 8, so it's too early to judge. No changes, no new podcast episode yet.

title: Model changes allowed: a wider network is queued (attempt 6)
text: You gave me freedom to change the model itself. The first change: more capacity. The shared leg controller has only 32 hidden neurons. Attempt 6 widens the current champion to 64 using the Net2Net trick: the new neurons start with zero outgoing weights, so the wider network walks exactly like the original (checked: same 272.79 on the replay track), and evolution then learns how to use the extra neurons. Only the size changes, so it can be compared fairly with attempt 5 (extra effort cost). It starts automatically when attempt 4's walk-fast stage ends. Other model changes I can try next: two hidden layers, a memory (recurrent) layer, or repeating each action for two steps.

title: Cheaper steps are winning: 279 with no falls
text: Attempt 4's walk-fast stage stopped on a plateau at 17:28, and attempt 6 (the widened network) started automatically. On the goal check's twenty independent tracks, the current champions compare like this. Attempt 5, where effort counts one and a half times in training: 279.4 points, no falls, 117 front-foot changes per run, effort 84, finishing in about 991 steps. Attempt 4's final walker: 260.8 with 2 falls; it finishes faster, in 954 steps, but takes more risks. Attempt 6, 64 neurons, still early at generation 59: 260.3 with 2 falls. All three meet the goal, and all of them have cut effort from about 99 to about 84. The extra effort cost looks like the most useful change so far. Both runs keep training; if attempt 5 keeps its lead, the next experiment will combine it with the wider network.

title: Attempt 7 combines the wider network with cheaper steps
text: Attempt 5, where effort counts one and a half times in training, has stopped improving: plus 4.6 points over 200 generations and a step size of 0.011. Its champion is the best walker so far, 284 on the held-out tracks and 279.4 on the goal check, with no falls, although foot 2 now leads a bit more often, about 61% of the time. Rather than wait two hours for the plateau rule, I stopped it and started attempt 7 from that champion: widened to 64 neurons the same way as attempt 6, keeping the 1.5 times effort cost. Attempt 6 (64 neurons from attempt 4's walker) keeps running alongside at 277 held-out.

title: The winner's curse, again: attempt 8 selects more carefully
text: The goal check, on twenty tracks no champion was chosen on, exposed a familiar problem. Attempt 5's newer champion looked better during selection but scored 270.6 with two falls on the goal tracks, while its earlier champion had 279.4 with none. Attempt 6's latest champion fell three times and scored 250.0, failing the safe requirement. At this level falls are rare, and scoring each candidate on five tracks and each champion on twenty picks lucky walkers. The best walker now is attempt 7's: the wider network with the extra effort cost, 284.4 on the goal check, no falls, 112 front-foot changes per run, finishing in about 941 steps. Attempt 6 had converged, so I stopped it and started attempt 8 from attempt 7's champion, with ten tracks per candidate and forty selection tracks, to make the choices more reliable.

title: Correction: the faster walkers fall more than the 20-track check showed
text: I have to correct last night's headline. On twenty goal-check tracks, the wider network with cheaper steps scored 288 with no falls. On a hundred comparison tracks it scores 262.9, give or take 63, and falls on fourteen of them. The precision run's champion is the same: 267.0 with twelve falls, and the difference between the two is noise. Both walkers really are faster, finishing in about 880 steps, and cheaper, with effort about 73. But yesterday afternoon's walker scored 263.9 with a spread of only one point and no falls in a hundred, finishing in about 1,100 steps. So the speed was bought with safety, and the average hasn't improved. The lesson, once more, is the winner's curse: twenty tracks are too few when falls are rare. Changes: the goal check now uses fifty tracks and allows at most ten percent falls; the wider network's run is stopped; and attempt 9 starts from it with falls costing double in training, to buy the safety back without losing the speed. The precision run continues alongside.

title: Safety paid: 285 on 100 tracks with 2 falls (new best, verified)
text: Making a fall cost double in training worked. Attempt 9's champion scores 284.7 on a hundred comparison tracks with only two falls, against 262.9 with fourteen falls for the walker it started from: a difference of about 22 points with a 95% interval of +8 to +36, better on 65 of 100 tracks. On the 50-track goal check it scores 282.8 with two falls (4%), 109 front-foot changes per run, lopsidedness 0.08, effort 75, finishing in about 914 steps. It also beats the old skipping walker's 270.2 on the same hundred tracks, with real alternating steps. Two other things: the precision run (attempt 8) converged with too many falls and was stopped, and a second hidden layer failed: the deeper network walked like the original but was so fragile that even tiny random changes made most candidates fall, so evolution couldn't fine-tune it. Next: attempt 10 starts from the new best with a fall costing three times as much, to see if more safety pays further.

title: Lucky champions, a lost walker, and a fix
text: Both safety runs reported new champions around 292 on their forty selection tracks. On a hundred comparison tracks they were worse: 268.2 with fourteen falls, and 234.0 with twenty five falls. They were individual candidates that happened to survive those forty tracks: faster, but riskier. The search's average walkers did better: 267.1 with fourteen falls and 273.5 with ten. Worse, the verified best walker from three hours ago, 284.7 with two falls, had been replaced as champion, and its exact parameters are gone; the nearest saved copy, one generation later, scores only 258.3 with eighteen falls, which shows how sensitive these walkers are. Fixes: every champion is now archived and can always be re-tested; new runs choose their champion from the search's average walker only, on sixty tracks. Attempts 11 and 12 start from the best walker we still have (273.5, ten falls on a hundred tracks) and differ only in the fall cost, three hundred versus two hundred.

title: Paused here: the final walker
text: The project is paused at the user's request, with a result they're happy with. Final walker: attempt 11's champion, a shared leg controller with a clock and 64 hidden neurons, trained with the curriculum (training wheels, then walking fast), a 1.5 times effort cost, falls costing three times in training, and champions chosen from the search's average walker. On a hundred comparison tracks it scores 281.8, give or take 38, with four falls, against 270.2 with seven falls for the old skipping walker on the same tracks. It finishes in about 900 steps, changes its leading foot about a hundred times per run with each foot leading half the time, and spends about 73 on motor effort. On the fifty-track goal check it meets all four requirements: 277.0, four falls in fifty, about 102 front-foot changes, lopsidedness 0.07. It is saved in the repository under models/final-walker, so it can't be overwritten. All training is stopped with checkpoints, so any run can be resumed later.
